title: Ghost branches: 40 remote branches that no longer exist
summary: Merged branches get deleted on the server, but your clone keeps showing them forever. Clean up the remote-tracking refs and the local branches whose upstream is gone.
mental_model: `origin/feature-x` is a local file recording what the server had. Deleting the branch on the server does not delete your file — only a prune does. Everything stale in `git branch -r` is a leftover snapshot.

steps.title: See branches that no longer exist on the server
steps.why: Both feature branches were deleted on the server during the setup, yet your clone lists them confidently. `git branch -r` is a cache, and nothing has invalidated it.

steps.title: A plain fetch does not help
steps.why: `fetch` adds and updates refs. It does not delete them, because deletion is destructive and git wants to be asked. This is why clones accumulate ghosts for years.
steps.expect: Exactly the same list. Nothing was cleaned up.

steps.title: Prune, and watch them disappear
steps.why: `--prune` deletes remote-tracking refs whose branch is gone on the server. This touches only your cache — no branch, local or remote, is affected.

verify.label: the stale remote-tracking refs are gone

steps.title: Find local branches whose upstream vanished
steps.why: Pruning does not delete your local branches — they still exist, now marked `gone`. That marker is the reliable signal that a branch was merged and cleaned up on the server.

steps.title: Delete the merged one safely
steps.why: `branch -d` accepts it because the work is in main. The abandoned one will be refused, which is exactly the distinction you want a tool to make for you.
steps.expect: First succeeds, second refuses — its commit is in no other branch.

verify.label: the merged local branch is deleted
the unmerged one was protected by -d

steps.title: Script the cleanup
steps.why: This one-liner deletes every local branch whose upstream is gone and which is fully merged. It is the standard end-of-sprint tidy-up, and it is safe precisely because it uses `-d` rather than `-D`.
commands: sh -c "git branch -vv | grep ': gone]' | awk '{print $1}' | xargs -r git branch -d"
steps.expect: Nothing further deleted — the abandoned branch is still unmerged, and -d protects it.

steps.title: Make pruning automatic
steps.why: `fetch.prune true` means every fetch and pull cleans up. There is essentially no downside: a pruned ref reappears the moment the branch does.

verify.label: pruning happens on every fetch now
the merged local branch was cleaned up
the unmerged branch survived — -d refuses to lose work

pitfalls: Pruning never deletes commits or local branches. It only removes your cached view of remote branches.
`git remote prune origin --dry-run` shows what would go, if you want to look before pruning.
A branch marked `gone` may have been renamed rather than merged. Check `git log` before deleting anything with `-D`.
In a repository with hundreds of contributors, `git branch -a` without pruning is unusable. Turn `fetch.prune` on once and forget it.
cheatsheet: drop remote-tracking refs for deleted branches
